analysis.one_liner: Created an SEC office to directly oversee audits of risky public companies.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to committee in July 2002 and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron and WorldCom accounting scandals, this bill would have created an Office of Audit Review inside the SEC with power to supervise audits of public companies deemed high-risk, require auditor rotation every three years, review auditor consulting deals, and fund itself through fees on public companies. It died in committee without a hearing or vote, while the narrower Sarbanes-Oxley Act became law two days after it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirement savers, pension holders, and employees whose savings depend on accurate corporate financial statements; also smaller audit firms that could win business under mandatory auditor rotation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors, pension holders, and company employees

how_it_helps.text: The SEC office could participate in and supervise all stages of a covered company's audit, review work papers before, during, and after the audit, and question audit committees and independent auditors [S3].
Covered companies would have to switch audit firms every three years, weakening the long-term client relationships that were seen as compromising auditor independence [S3].
The office could review any agreement under which the auditor also sells consulting or other non-audit services to the company it audits [S3].
The SEC would set risk-based criteria for which companies face enhanced oversight, including size, recent mergers, and circumstances posing a high risk of business failure or wrongdoing [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public companies and their shareholders, who would bear the cost of the self-financing office through fees assessed on companies filing financial statements and collected through their audit firms [S3].

drawbacks.text: Government supervising every stage of a private audit is a large expansion of SEC power that could slow audits, raise compliance costs, and blur responsibility if a supervised audit still missed fraud [S3].
A three-year forced auditor rotation could cost companies institutional knowledge of their books and shift fees to fee-paying public companies, whose shareholders ultimately bear these costs [S3].
The bill's risk criteria were broad and discretionary, covering everything from labor relations to marketing programs, which invited lobbying over which companies were designated high-risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — a government watchdog inside the audit process for the riskiest companies, with a ban on multi-service conflicts and auditor rotation — targeted exactly the conflicts that let Enron's and WorldCom's books stay clean on paper while they collapsed. The costs are real but modest: higher audit and compliance expenses for public companies and slower audits. The main design weakness is breadth and discretion, which the SEC would have had to fill with rulemaking. It was a serious reform response to a genuine crisis.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced July 23, 2002, referred to the House Financial Services Committee and then to a subcommittee on August 19, and received no further action before Congress adjourned in January 2003 [S5, S1].

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 23, 2002, and referred the same day to the House Financial Services Committee [S5].
It was referred to the Capital Markets, Insurance and Government Sponsored Enterprises subcommittee on August 19, 2002, and no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded [S5].

Two days after introduction, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act — a different, narrower accounting reform that created a private-sector oversight board rather than direct SEC supervision — was signed into law [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Congress passed and President Bush signed the narrower Sarbanes-Oxley Act instead, and the big accounting firms and public companies kept audit oversight in private-sector and self-regulatory channels rather than direct SEC supervision. Investors got some new protections but not the direct government supervision of audits this bill proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large audit firms and public companies

for.name: Danny K. Davis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the House floor; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill; it was referred to a subcommittee on August 19 and never scheduled for a hearing or markup [S5].

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor, and two days after its introduction the Sarbanes-Oxley Act was enacted instead as the chamber's response to accounting fraud [S1].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded votes, so no party split can be measured [S4, S5].

industries.note: Mandatory three-year auditor rotation, SEC supervision of audit work papers, and fee collection through the firms threatened the lucrative long-term client relationships and consulting arrangements that made the largest firms' audits profitable. It would have subjected their work to direct government review [S3].
Companies deemed high-risk would face government supervision of every stage of their audits, forced auditor rotation, and fees to fund the new office, raising compliance costs for shareholders [S3].
